passage: By eleven each morning, Jagdish was already tired. The open-plan floor at the Bengaluru office rang with phones and chatter, and every coffee trip meant small talk about weekend plans he didn't have. The work itself he loved. Give him a messy dataset and a clear question, and he would vanish into it for hours. The trouble came with messages like "Make the report more punchy." On Friday he wrote to his manager, Manoj: "I work best with written tasks and a clear definition of done. Could I also use the quiet room in the afternoons?" Manoj replied within the hour. "Of course. I'll put tasks in writing from Monday. Tell me what else helps." Jagdish read it twice, then leaned back and let out a long breath.

qa.q: What did Jagdish ask to use in the afternoons?
qa.a: The quiet room.

qa.q: How did Jagdish feel after reading Manoj's reply, and what shows it?
qa.a: He felt relieved; he read it twice, leaned back and let out a long breath.

qa.q: What turning point improved Jagdish's working week?
qa.a: He clearly asked in writing for written tasks, a definition of done and use of the quiet room, instead of struggling silently.

qa.q: How might Manoj see the request from a manager's side?
qa.a: Manoj seems to see it as reasonable and useful, since clearer instructions help Jagdish do the work he is good at.

grounding: It shows an adult drained by open-plan noise, small talk and vague requests, who thrives with clear written tasks and feels relief when an adjustment is granted.

passage: "So Saturday. Maybe brunch, maybe the market, we'll see how we feel?" Sonali said, stirring her tea. Ishita put her cup down. "Can I tell you something about 'we'll see'?" "Uh oh." "No, it's fine. When plans are open like that, I spend the whole week running every version in my head. By Saturday I'm tired before we leave the flat." "I didn't know that." "I didn't say it before. I thought it would sound strange. But you're my closest person, and I'd rather you know." Sonali was quiet, then pulled a notepad from the drawer. "Okay. Saturday. Brunch at eleven. Market after, one hour. Home by three. Better?" "Much better." Ishita laughed, a little shakily. "Thank you for not calling it silly." "It isn't silly. Now I actually know how to plan with you."

qa.q: What time did Sonali write down for brunch?
qa.a: Eleven.

qa.q: Why did Ishita not mention the problem with open plans before?
qa.a: She thought it would sound strange and was worried about how Sonali would react.

qa.q: What choice made the Saturday plan work for both of them?
qa.a: Ishita explained her need honestly, and Sonali wrote down a clear plan with times instead of leaving it open.

qa.q: How does Sonali's view of their weekends change after the talk?
qa.a: Sonali now understands why open plans tire Ishita and finally knows how to plan with Ishita.

grounding: It shows an adult for whom unclear plans are draining, who asks for a clear plan in a close relationship and feels relief at being understood.

passage:
Subject: Working in the way I work best
Dear Pradeep,
Thank you for the first three weeks. I want to be honest about what helps me do my best work.
The open floor is very loud for me. By afternoon I find it hard to think. Could I sit at the desk near the back wall, or wear noise-cancelling headphones?
Spoken instructions in stand-ups slip away from me. If tasks could be written in the tracker, I will finish them faster and with fewer questions.
I sometimes skip the team lunch. It is not because I don't like the team; small talk tires me out.
I really enjoy the data cleaning project. I'd like to keep it.
Best,
Kiran

qa.q: What project does Kiran enjoy?
qa.a: Kiran enjoys the data cleaning project.

qa.q: How does Kiran feel on the open floor by the afternoon?
qa.a: Kiran feels drained and finds it hard to think, because the open floor is very loud.

qa.q: Why is Kiran's email a sensible way to ask for help?
qa.a: It is clear and specific, explains the reasons and suggests small adjustments, like a quieter desk and written tasks, that help Kiran work well.

qa.q: How might Pradeep see Kiran after reading the email?
qa.a: Pradeep may see Kiran as a committed colleague who knows how to work best, and realise the team lunch absence is not unfriendliness.

grounding: Shows a young adult who finds open offices, small talk and unclear instructions draining but works well with clear written tasks, and reasonably asks for adjustments.

passage: So you asked how the new job is going. Honestly? The first month I came home and lay on the floor every night. The office is one big hall, people chat by the kettle, and my manager, Francis, would say things like "just make it pop." I had no idea what that meant. I thought I was failing. Then I told him, "I'm autistic, and I work best with written steps." I was shaking when I said it. He just nodded and said, "Okay, what would help?" Now every task comes in a list with a deadline. I have a desk by the window. I'm Jasleen, and for the first time at work I feel understood. It's such a relief.

qa.q: What did Francis say when Jasleen explained the best way to work?
qa.a: He nodded and said, "Okay, what would help?"

qa.q: How did Jasleen feel when Francis responded kindly?
qa.a: Jasleen felt relieved and understood, after being scared enough to shake while telling him.

qa.q: What made the adjustment easy once Jasleen spoke up?
qa.a: Francis asked what would help, then gave written task lists with deadlines and a quieter desk by the window.

qa.q: How does Francis seem to see Jasleen's request?
qa.a: Francis seems to see it as simple and reasonable; he just asks what would help and then gives written lists and a quieter desk.

grounding: Shows an autistic adult drained by an open office and vague instructions, who asks for reasonable adjustments and feels relief at being understood.

passage:
Week one: Pooja started at the design studio in Hyderabad. The open hall buzzed all day. Every morning her team lead, Harish, asked, "Weekend plans?" and she froze. At home she sat in the dark till dinner.
Week three: Pooja wrote Harish a short message. "I do my best work with clear written briefs, a quiet corner and fewer surprise meetings." She sent it, then paced for an hour.
Week six: Briefs now come on a shared page. Pooja sits in the small room by the plants. Harish just says "Morning" and moves on. She finished the brochure layout two days early, and Harish told the client, "Pooja's work is always exact." She went home and cooked dinner, humming.

qa.q: Where does Pooja sit by week six?
qa.a: She sits in the small room by the plants.

qa.q: How did Pooja feel right after sending the message in week three?
qa.a: She felt anxious and nervous, pacing for an hour after sending it.

qa.q: Which change helped Pooja most, and why?
qa.a: Clear written briefs and a quiet corner let her focus instead of struggling with noise and surprise talk, so she finished early.

qa.q: How might Harish see Pooja by week six?
qa.a: Harish sees her as precise and dependable; he praises her work to the client and is glad the adjustments help.

grounding: Shows a young adult drained by an open office and small talk who asks for adjustments and thrives with clear written tasks, relieved to be understood.

passage:
Sit, sit. You're new, so let me tell you about Naveen. Twenty years I've been in this firm, and I'm Ganga, the one who trained him.
Naveen joined at twenty-four, sharp as anything with code. But the open floor wore him out. The chatter, the phones, the Monday small talk. By four o'clock he'd be staring at the wall. His first manager called him moody.
Then one day he came to me with a typed page. "I work best with written tasks, a quieter desk and clear deadlines. Is that possible?"
Honestly, I was surprised. But I asked the manager, Suresh, to try it. Naveen moved to the corner near the server room. Suresh sent every task in writing.
Within a month, Naveen's work was the cleanest on the team. He told me, "Being understood is like putting down a heavy bag." Remember that, if you ever need to ask.

qa.q: Where did Naveen move his desk?
qa.a: To the corner near the server room.

qa.q: How did Naveen feel once the changes were made?
qa.a: He felt relieved and lighter, saying being understood is like putting down a heavy bag.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Naveen's typed request for written tasks, a quieter desk and clear deadlines; asking for reasonable adjustments let his real skills show.

qa.q: How might Suresh have seen Naveen after a month?
qa.a: Suresh probably saw him as one of the strongest people on the team, not moody, once the tasks were clear and written.

grounding: Ganga tells a new colleague how Naveen found the open office and small talk draining, asked for adjustments and thrived with written tasks.
